2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite. It must render one full-viewport canvas with id #app. The scene is a desert canyon at dusk: tall layered sandstone walls on both sides of a winding dry riverbed, warm orange and magenta low sun near the horizon, a cool blue-violet sky gradient overhead, long soft shadows, and a few scattered boulders and dead shrubs on the canyon floor. 2

I'm planning a canyon flythrough scene with a heightfield mesh showing layered strata via vertex colors, plus boulders, shrubs, lights, and a native sky/fog/camera animation. I'm designing a periodic centerline curve combining sine waves so the canyon path loops seamlessly for a continuous flythrough.

I need the terrain long enough that the camera's looping range stays well within its bounds, with fog hiding the far edges so the loop point and terrain boundaries are never visible—using a terrain span that extends beyond the camera's periodic movement range and view distance.

For boulders and shrubs, I'll generate them within one period and duplicate them at a few offsets so distant fog-visible props don't pop when the loop resets, keeping the height function itself periodic via integer-harmonic sinusoids. For the terrain mesh, I'm sizing resolution to keep vertex count safely under index limits while staying detailed enough.

Now I'm working out the canyon wall shape: a distance-from-centerline function with variable width, a flat riverbed floor near the center, and a steep exponential wall profile beyond it, then quantizing that height into terraced steps to get a layered rock-strata look.

I'm adding erosion-style noise bumps and coloring the strata bands with alternating ochre, red-orange, tan, and pale sandstone tones, capping both walls around 60m with a noisy plateau beyond. For the camera, I'm placing it about 2.5m above a 16-24m wide floor, drifting slightly side to side as it follows the winding canyon axis, with tall 40-60m walls at a 640x360 resolution and roughly 60° FOV. I'm setting dusk lighting with a low sun elevation around 6° angled to cast long shadows down the winding canyon.

I want the camera looking somewhat into the glare for drama, with warm horizon tones, upper walls catching orange light while lower walls stay shadowed, balanced by a cool violet ambient fill so the shadows don't go too dark. Now I need to check how the engine's fog and sky gradient systems work—matching fog color to the horizon gradient—and whether a golden-hour preset could serve as a starting point before I dig into the fog signature details.

content.thinking:
I'll go with the bridge approach for terrain and props using vertex colors, but keep lights native since that's simpler to tune. The recipe just needs meshes with a MeshStandardMaterial using vertex colors enabled, and I'll define the periodic z-axis geometry using a 2π phase variable over the 300-unit period.

Working out the centerline, half-width, and slope math for the terrain, I'm checking the worst-case slope stays manageable (~0.9) so the winding is gentle enough. I'm now designing the height function combining a noisy floor, a meandering dry riverbed channel, and steep tanh-based canyon walls with ledges.

For the walls, I want roughly 45m rise over 20m horizontal with 60-75° steepness, using an exponential rise function and then terracing it into stepped ledges by quantizing to a stratum height with smoothstep transitions, adding noise before terracing so the ledges aren't perfectly uniform.

Height varies with angular position plus noise, and far from the walls the terrain plateaus with gentle undulations of a few meters.

From a 2m-eye-height camera near the base, the 45m walls at close range will fill most of the vertical field of view, leaving only a narrow strip of visible sky.

I'm scaling things back a bit — lowering max wall height to around 30m and widening the canyon to 12-16m with a gentler vertical fov and slight upward pitch so the sky peeks through. I'm also working out the mesh resolution, picking grid spacing that keeps vertex count under the Uint16 index limit while still resolving the steep terraces, and figuring out how the terrain's z-range, camera looping, and fog falloff should interact.

I'm settling on an exponential fog density so distant walls fade convincingly by around 150m, and extending the terrain range to cover the camera's loop plus buffer. For the floor, I'm deciding to keep it mostly flat with small riverbed dips rather than trying to replicate the exact noise function natively, since the camera just needs an approximate height to sit on.

For camera motion, I'm giving it a lateral drift (3*sin(t*0.4)) around the centerline, which stays safely within the floor width, and now I'm thinking about keeping boulders clear of that drift path so they don't collide with the camera.

At 5 m/s the loop becomes 60 seconds for 300m, with the camera looking ahead along the path using a smoothed lead point so the yaw stays gentle as z wraps seamlessly—though I need the drift's sine period to align with the loop duration so the wrap doesn't introduce a visible jump.

For boulders I'm using flattened icosahedrons with per-vertex displacement and color, writing my own geometry-merging function to combine all ~90 copies into a single BufferGeometry with vertex colors rather than relying on external imports, since separate meshes would be fine draw-call-wise but merging keeps things cleaner.

For shrubs I'm building tapered cylinder branches recursively (two levels deep, roughly seven branches each), applying transforms via composed matrices and normal matrices, then appending each transformed geometry's position, normal, and color data into shared arrays, handling indexed geometry with proper offsets.

For boulders, I'm using low-detail icosahedrons (non-indexed, so normals come out flat-shaded for a nice faceted rock look), displacing vertices with a noise function based on direction before recomputing normals — keeping total triangle counts manageable across ~30 boulders. I'm picking a greyish-brown for dead shrubs and a sandstone tone for boulders.

For terrain coloring, I'm placing boulders at the actual terrain height function rather than a simplified offset, and banding the terrain colors by elevation through a cycling palette of rust and tan tones, blending between bands for a gradual strata effect.

For the floor, I'm using pale sand colors with a lighter riverbed tone, blending toward darker talus near the walls. Flat ledges get a dusty tan overlay based on surface normal, while steep faces show the full rock strata pattern.

Switching to color management, I'm setting hex colors through THREE.Color so sRGB gets converted to linear internally, matching how glTF expects vertex colors. For lighting, I'm planning a warm orange directional sun at low angle coming from ahead-left, and now I need to check how the shadow frustum settings work for a scene this large—looking into the directional shadow options and whether it should track the camera.
